noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: understand that bond breaking can be: i homolytic, to produce free radicals ii heterolytic, to produce ions

primer.text: A covalent bond can split its shared pair in two ways, and the split decides everything that follows. Heterolytic fission hands both electrons to one atom and births ions; homolytic fission deals one electron to each and births free radicals. This note defines both cuts and the dot notation that marks the radicals.

lessons.title: Heterolytic fission: the one-sided split
lessons.opening: When a covalent bond breaks, the shared pair must go somewhere. Heterolytic fission hands the entire pair to the more electronegative atom, so ions appear where the bond was - a positive cation and a negative anion, ready for the ionic mechanisms that follow.
keyPoints: Heterolytic fission breaks a covalent bond so both bonding electrons go to one atom.
The more electronegative atom takes the pair and becomes a negative ion.
The electron-starved partner becomes a positive ion (a cation).
Bond breaking can be homolytic (radicals) or heterolytic (ions) - the split decides the products.
Electronegativity difference in the bond usually predicts which way heterolytic fission runs.

low.restatement: In heterolytic fission one atom walks off with the whole shared pair: the taker becomes negative, the loser becomes positive, and both products are ions.
low.analogy: A couple dissolving a joint account where one partner keeps every coin: one leaves wealthy (anion), the other empty (cation).
low.examPointer: Show both charges and both products in equations - an ionic fission answer missing either ion drops a mark.

medium.restatement: The direction of the split follows the polarisation already present: the delta-negative end of a polar bond is the natural pair-keeper, which is why H-X bonds fission to X(-) plus H(+).
medium.analogy: The pre-existing tilt of the seesaw decides which side everything slides to when the middle support snaps.
medium.examPointer: Connect heterolytic fission to the electrophilic addition mechanism - the carbocation and bromide of that mechanism are exactly this fission's products.

check.stem: What distinguishes heterolytic fission from homolytic fission?

options.text: Heterolytic gives both electrons to one atom; homolytic gives one to each
options.explanation: The pair's destination defines the names.
Only the bond's electron pair is redistributed.
UV is the homolytic trigger, not the heterolytic one.
Radicals are homolytic products.

check.stem: Which species results when a bond breaks heterolytically toward the more electronegative atom?

options.text: A negative ion on the electronegative atom and a positive ion on the other
options.explanation: The pair-keeper goes negative; the loser goes positive.
That is the homolytic outcome.
Charge cannot be created - one loss, one gain.
Ions are the signature of heterolytic fission.

check.stem: In heterolytic fission of H-Br, where do the bonding electrons go?

options.text: To bromine, giving Br(-) and H(+)
options.explanation: Bromine's higher electronegativity takes the pair.

options.text: To hydrogen, giving H(-) and Br(+)
options.explanation: Hydrogen is the less electronegative partner.
Even splitting is homolysis.
The pair goes to an atom, not the medium.

check.stem: What does the atom that loses the shared pair become?

options.text: A cation, an electron-starved positive ion
options.explanation: Losing the pair leaves a charge deficit.
Radicals come from one-electron splits.
Anion means it gained the pair.
Its electron count changed, so its charge changed.

check.stem: Why does electronegativity predict heterolytic direction?

options.text: The more electronegative atom already pulls the pair closer, so it keeps it when the bond breaks
options.explanation: Polarisation pre-stages the split.
It measures electron-pulling power.
It applies across covalent bonds.
It is the standard predictor of the split.

check.stem: Define heterolytic fission and name both products in general terms.
check.modelAnswer: Heterolytic fission breaks a covalent bond so both bonding electrons go to one atom, producing a positive ion (cation) and a negative ion (anion).

check.stem: Write the heterolytic fission equation for H-Br and label each product.
check.modelAnswer: H-Br -> H(+) + Br(-): the hydrogen becomes the cation and bromine the anion.

check.stem: Explain why the products of heterolytic fission are reactive.
check.modelAnswer: The products are ions carrying full charges, so each is a ready donor or acceptor of electron pairs - the nucleophile and electrophile pairing that drives ionic mechanisms.

check.stem: A polar bond A-B breaks with both electrons going to B. State the charge and role of each fragment.
check.modelAnswer: B becomes the anion B(-) and acts as a nucleophile (pair donor); A becomes the cation A(+) and acts as an electrophile (pair acceptor).

lessons.title: Homolytic fission: the fair split
lessons.opening: Give the shared pair back to both partners - one electron each - and the products are free radicals: neutral fragments carrying unpaired electrons, written with a single dot. Ultraviolet light supplies the energy that persuades bonds like Cl-Cl to split this way.
keyPoints: Homolytic fission breaks a covalent bond so each atom receives one bonding electron.
The products are free radicals: neutral species with an unpaired electron.
A free radical is written with a single dot after its symbol, such as Cl•.
Ultraviolet light typically supplies the energy that drives homolytic fission.
The chlorine molecule splits as Cl2 -> 2Cl• under UV - the classic initiation step.

low.restatement: In homolytic fission the pair is divided evenly: each fragment keeps one electron, becomes a neutral radical, and carries its unpaired electron as a dot in the equation.
low.analogy: A fair divorce settlement: the shared estate (the pair) is split in half, each partner leaving with one item and a visible tag (the dot).
low.examPointer: Draw the dot on every radical - missing dots lose the notation mark in every radical mechanism question.

medium.restatement: The unpaired electron makes radicals desperate to pair again, which is why they extract hydrogens or combine with each other; UV light provides the bond energy that homolysis of Cl-Cl requires.
medium.analogy: Each radical is a half-mitten hunting its match; sunlight is the price of admission to the hunt.
medium.examPointer: State both the condition (UV) and the notation (dot) whenever homolytic fission appears - the specification pairs them.

options.text: A neutral species carrying an unpaired electron
options.explanation: The unpaired electron defines it.

options.text: A charged ion with a full octet
options.explanation: Radicals are neutral and electron-short.

options.text: A molecule with all electrons paired
options.explanation: Paired electrons mean no radical.
That is an ionic species, not a radical.

check.stem: How is a chlorine free radical written?

options.text: Cl•, with a single dot for the unpaired electron
options.explanation: The dot is the radical's signature.
That is the chloride ion.
That would be a cation.
The dot must appear for the radical.

check.stem: Which condition typically drives homolytic fission of chlorine?

options.explanation: UV supplies the energy to split the Cl-Cl bond evenly.
Nickel serves hydrogenation.
Acids serve ionic mechanisms.
Darkness prevents the radical route.

check.stem: What products form when a chlorine molecule undergoes homolytic fission?

options.explanation: One electron each - two identical radicals.
That is heterolytic fission.
The bond breaks, so the molecule no longer exists.
A mixed pair is not an even split.

options.text: Their unpaired electron seeks a partner to pair with
options.explanation: Electron hunger drives the attack on other bonds.
They are neutral.
Size is not the reactivity driver.
Stability contradicts reactivity.

check.stem: Define homolytic fission and write the equation for chlorine undergoing it.
check.modelAnswer: Homolytic fission splits a covalent bond with one electron going to each atom, forming radicals: Cl2 -> 2Cl• under ultraviolet light.

check.stem: State what notation marks a radical and what energy source typically starts homolytic fission.
check.modelAnswer: A single dot marks the unpaired electron, and ultraviolet light typically supplies the energy for the split.

check.stem: Explain why homolytic rather than heterolytic fission occurs in a non-polar bond like Cl-Cl.
check.modelAnswer: The identical atoms share the pair evenly, so there is no electronegativity tilt to hand the pair to one side - the symmetric bond breaks symmetrically when energy is supplied.

check.stem: Bromine gas is irradiated with ultraviolet light. Write the homolytic fission equation with correct radical notation and state what each product carries.
check.modelAnswer: Br2 -> 2Br•: each bromine radical is a neutral atom carrying one unpaired electron, marked by the single dot.

glossary.definition: Bond breaking in which both bonding electrons go to one atom, producing a cation and an anion.
Bond breaking in which each atom receives one bonding electron, producing free radicals.
A neutral species carrying an unpaired electron, written with a single dot.
